desc:
Decide whether the array nums can be cut into consecutive blocks so that every block has one of these three shapes:

  • two equal elements, such as [7,7];
  • three equal elements, such as [5,5,5];
  • three elements that go up by exactly 1 each step, such as [4,5,6].

Every element must belong to exactly one block. Return true if such a cutting exists, otherwise false.

nums = [4,4,4,5,6]  -> true    ([4,4] and [4,5,6])
nums = [1,1,1,2]    -> false   (no cutting works)
nums = [3,4,5]      -> true    (one block of three consecutive values)
hints: Look at the end of the array. Which block shapes could be the last block, and what remains in front of them?
Let ok[i] be true when the first i elements can be cut into valid blocks, with ok[0] = true.
ok[i] is true if (ok[i-2] and the last two elements are equal) or (ok[i-3] and the last three elements are all equal or form x, x+1, x+2). The answer is ok[n].
editorial: A prefix DP works because a block has a fixed small length. Let ok[i] tell whether the first i elements can be cut into valid blocks; the empty prefix is fine, so ok[0] = true. The last block of a good prefix is a pair of equal elements (then ok[i-2] must hold) or a triple of equal or consecutive-increasing elements (then ok[i-3] must hold).

Each state looks at the previous two or three states, so one pass in O(n) time suffices; keeping only the last three booleans reduces memory to O(1). A greedy rule such as 'always take a triple first' fails: [1,1,1,1] needs two pairs, while [1,1,1,2,3] needs a pair and a run, not a triple of ones.
